prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the sewing machine and tabletop directly in front of the camera wearer, with the machine roughly 0.4–0.8 m away, the wearer’s hands about 0.3–0.6 m away, and the far edge of the table and standing person roughly 1–2 m away; the floor and background extend farther behind them. It clarifies the vertical layering that is less obvious in RGB: hands and forearms are above and nearer than the table, while the machine sits on the table and partly blocks the farther person’s lower body. Across the five frames, the wearer’s right hand moves from low and central toward the machine’s upper-right area and becomes markedly nearer in frame 5, while the left hand enters near the lower centre in frame 4; the machine remains at nearly constant range. The map is unreliable around thin structures, object boundaries, the black upper background, and the hands, with abrupt halos and merged surfaces making exact distances and separations uncertain.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates the camera wearer’s visible arms and hands as person regions in the lower half, showing their spread from left/centre toward the sewing machine and their partial truncation by the bottom and right image borders. It also intermittently marks a farther person near the top of frames 4–5, roughly 1–2 m from the camera and behind the table, and labels large upper objects as suitcase and skateboard even though those classes do not agree with the RGB scene. Relative to the camera wearer, the machine is directly ahead and slightly left of the right hand, while the blue container or cloth lies to the machine’s right, but neither is reliably segmented as its visible object class. Across time, the wearer’s arm mask expands upward and rightward as the hand approaches the machine, while the other hand appears near the lower centre in frame 4; fragmented masks, missing objects, implausible labels, and merged person regions make distance, facing direction, and inter-person separation unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map localizes only hands: one magenta hand skeleton stays near the lower-centre/right area in frames 1, 2, and 4, another extended hand appears above the machine in frame 3, and a hand appears high on the right in frame 5. These keypoints clarify finger orientation and hand rotation against the cluttered machine: the frame-3 hand extends from left toward the centre/right, the lower hands are oriented upward toward the machine, and the frame-5 hand is raised near the machine’s upper-right side, all within roughly 0.3–0.7 m of the camera wearer. No dependable body skeleton is present for the farther person, so the map cannot establish that person’s full posture, facing direction, gaze, or reach; the RGB only suggests that this person is partly out of view above the table. The changing hand locations show approach and turning of the wearer’s hands across frames, but missing wrists or arms, isolated detections, and the absence of many visible hands make continuity, occlusion, and exact reach estimates unreliable.
